title: When Laugh-O-gram Ran Out of Money in Kansas City, 1923
dek: Walt Disney's first studio failed within about a year, leaving unpaid staff and investors with nothing, and he left for California with one short film.

story.event: Bankruptcy of his first animation studio and his departure for California
story.summary: Laugh-O-gram Films, incorporated in Kansas City in May 1922 with money from local investors and Walt Disney as president, failed after its distributor, Pictorial Clubs, paid only $100 of a contract for six cartoons and went bankrupt. The company went into bankruptcy in 1923; Disney left for California that August with the short Alice's Wonderland and in October signed a contract for a series of Alice comedies. Creditors received 45 cents on the dollar in 1927 and the investors nothing.
paragraphs: In the last months of Laugh-O-gram Films, Walt Disney, by then 21, slept in the office of his own company in Kansas City. He ate on credit at a Greek restaurant on the ground floor, lived partly on occasional $30 cheques from his brother Roy, and paid a dime to bathe at the railway station. The company had been incorporated in May 1922, with Disney as president and $15,000 from local investors.

Its problem was a contract. In September 1922 Pictorial Clubs agreed to take six cartoons, paying $100 at signing and about $11,000 more only after all six were delivered, in January 1924. Pictorial went bankrupt within months without paying the rest. By the end of 1922 the crew was working unpaid and several people had left; one animator wrote to his parents that the business was "worse than broke".

Disney kept looking for something that would save it. "I was desperately trying to get something that would take hold, catch on," he later said. In spring 1923 he made Alice's Wonderland, a short that set a real four-year-old girl, Virginia Davis, among cartoon figures, and wrote to the New York distributor Margaret Winkler that his team had "discovered something new and clever in animated cartoons". Roy's advice was blunter: "Kid, I think you should get out of there." He was evicted from his rooms for unpaid rent, and the company went into bankruptcy. The last money he earned in Kansas City, for filming a six-month-old girl, paid for his train ticket. In August 1923 he left for California, riding first class, he recalled, in trousers and a coat that did not match.

He meant to become a film director and was, he said, "fed up with cartoons". But on 16 October 1923 he signed a contract with Winkler for a series of Alice comedies, and he and Roy set up the studio that became the Walt Disney Company. Several Kansas City animators, among them Ub Iwerks, Hugh Harman and Rudolf Ising, followed him west. Those who had backed Laugh-O-gram fared worse. Its creditors waited until 1927 and received 45 cents on the dollar; the investors received nothing.

quote.text: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi pairs each loss with its turning: the partial made whole, the emptied thing filled. Disney left Kansas City with no company and one short film from its last months, and it was that small piece of work, not the studio, that carried over.

reflection: There are two true ways to read Laugh-O-gram. One is the familiar one: a young man loses his company, keeps one good idea and starts again. The other belongs to the investors who got nothing back and the animators who worked unpaid through a Kansas City winter. Neither cancels the other.

If something you started has gone badly, you may feel you must choose between excusing yourself and condemning yourself. You do not have to. You can be honest about what it cost other people, put right what you are able to, and still carry forward the one part of it that worked.
invitation: Think of one thing you began that did not work out. Write down the single part of it still worth keeping, and let the rest stay where it is for today.

research_notes: Bankruptcy dates disagree. MousePlanet (Korkis) and The Pendergast Years say Laugh-O-gram filed in July 1923, with the process finalised in October; a summary of the National Archives case file (case 4457) published by the American Bankruptcy Institute says Ub Iwerks filed a creditor's petition on 4 October 1923, with schedules on 13 November 1923; a Kansas City Public Library timeline says the company declared bankruptcy on 30 October 1923; D23 says simply that Walt 'declared bankruptcy'. Both the ABI and National Archives pages were blocked or down for automated requests, so the story says only that the company went into bankruptcy before Disney left in August and does not say who filed; it also avoids D23's wording, since the debtor was the company, not Walt personally. Incorporation is given as 18 May (MousePlanet), 23 May (Pendergast) and 22 May 1922 in other summaries; the story says May 1922. Contract value: $11,000 balance plus $100 down (MousePlanet) versus $11,100 total (Merritt and Kaufman, Pendergast); these agree, and the story says $100 plus about $11,000. The widely repeated claim that Disney arrived in California with $40 could not be traced to a reliable loadable source and is left out, as is the story that a dental film earned $500. The 45-cents settlement in 1927 and the investors receiving nothing rest on MousePlanet alone (Korkis cites the trustee's settlement with Pictorial; Susanin's Walt Before Mickey covers it in print); they are stated plainly because they matter to the people who lost money. Funding is set to venture rather than the slate's bootstrapped because the company raised about $15,000 from outside local investors. The Laozi line is applied by analogy; Legge's chapter goes on to praise having few desires.
